newsitem.title: UK: Oil price rally pauses but fundamentals remain strong.
newsitem.headline: Oil price rally pauses but fundamentals remain strong.

text.p: A rally in world oil prices paused for breath on Friday as traders rounded off a volatile week with a spurt of profit-taking.
But the market remained strong and the modest selloff was expected after a week-long rally took prices for heating oil and diesel to five-year highs on Thursday, traders said.

Although tension in the Middle East has lent support, the oil market's main support has come from the rush to top up extremely low stocks of heating fuel before the peak winter demand period, they said.
"The most significant market is still heating oil, crude is following its lead on both sides of the Atlantic," said one dealer.
Benchmark Brent November crude futures were trading seven cents lower on the day at $22.86 a barrel by 1605 GMT. But prices are about $6 above 1995 levels.

"It's more of a retracement, we're still seeing good premiums for gas oil on the cash markets which makes me suspicious that the whole thing might go up again," said Christopher Bellew of London futures brokers Prudential Bache.
Traders said thin heating oil inventories both sides of the Atlantic were unusual for this time of year.
"Shortages are usually caused by a sudden cold snap which draws product from one side of the Atlantic to the other to compensate," Bellew said.
But this year, U.S. and European refiners alike have been caught short ahead of winter because of a cost-cutting decision to keep forward supplies to a minimum.
Heating oil stocks in the U.S. Central Atlantic, a key region around New York Harbor, are now more than a third lower than a year ago at 20 million barrels.
As a result, most traders are betting that oil prices will rise further.
"This market is still in an uptrend, whatever we're seeing today," one trader said.
Meanwhile, world oil markets have largely shrugged off Israeli-Palestinian violence, with traders seeing no immediate threat to Gulf oil supplies.

But oil analysts said on Friday that continued bloodshed in the West Bank and Gaza Strip could scuttle the Middle East peace process and force oil-rich Gulf countries to rethink their already uneasy alliance with the U.S.

"This could lead to a medium-term change in attitude of the Arab countries' to the U.S. presence there and could undermine the stability of the Gulf," said John Mitchell, chairman of the Energy and Environmentral Programme at the Royal Institute of International Affairs.
